*Reproducibility based on ringtests*

When expert agreement on thresholds for equivalence cannot be obtained, a method to derive thresholds can be based on so-called inter-laboratory ringtests. 
Ringtests are described in an ISO-standard @iso57252025 and can be used to derive a measure of reproducibility of a certain lab method.
Reproducibility is composed of within-lab variability (repeatability) and between-lab variability.
In statistical notation, the variance can be written as the sum of the variance of both components:

$$
\sigma^2_R = \sigma^2_{\text{reproducibility}} = \sigma^2_{\text{repeatability}} + \sigma^2_{\text{inter-laboratory}}
$${#eq-ringtest}

Reproducibility of the SML reference methods for a soil descriptor can be measured through such a ringtest.
The thresholds to define equivalence of a non-reference method can then be based on the level of reproducibility of the reference method.
If the reference method $Y$ is reproducible up to a value of $\sigma^2_R$, then a non-reference method $X$ could be defined as equivalent if the difference has an expected value of 0 over the whole range of the soil descriptor and if the difference falls within a pre-defined range with a certain probability (for example a range of 2 times $\sigma^2_R$ with a probability of 95%):

$$
\begin{aligned}
D &= Y - X \\
E[D|X] &= 0 \\
P(D \in \pm k \sigma_R) &= 1 - \alpha
\end{aligned}
$${#eq-equivalence}

Ringtests that examine multiple samples spread over a large range of the soil descriptor allow to calculate the reproducibility in function of the value of the soil descriptor: $\sigma_R(Y)$.
Soil descriptors can have different levels of reproducibility for small or large values, often the reproducibility variance increases for larger values of the soil descriptor.
